Participants less likely to be followed up were those with low birthweight or short length at birth, those born by vaginal delivery, those whose mothers had low levels of education, were smokers or were young, and those whose heads of family were in manual occupations. The cohort currently comprises 1775 individuals. The data collected cover physical health (body composition, bone mineral density, pulmonary function, blood pressure, endothelial dysfunction, asthma, allergy, sleep health and oral health), mental health, biomarkers of genetic and epigenetic samples, nutrition, non-communicable diseases, physical activity, behavioural risk factors, domestic violence, socioeconomic status and human capital. Cohort data are available on request, with a description of the planned project, from [mabarbieri@fmrp.usp.br, hbettiol@fmrp.usp.br, or ferraro@usp.br]. In the 1970s and 1980s, there was no established research ethics committee to evaluate the projects. Permission was initially obtained from all clinical directors of maternity hospitals and registry offices and from the regional health department. In 1987–89, permission was obtained from the state and the municipal education secretariats. In the following three waves, the participants gave informed consent, and the project was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University Hospital of the Ribeirão Preto Medical School of the University of São Paulo (HCRP protocol No. 4866/96 in the 1996–97 follow-up; HCRP protocol No. 7606/99 in 2002–04; and HCRP protocol No. 2.998.903 in 2016–17). In 1978–79, the intentions were: (i) to describe the sociodemographic characteristics of the population and the medical care offered during pregnancy and birth, according to maternal age; (ii) to determine the rates of low birthweight, caesarean sections and infant mortality; and (iii) to determine possible risk factors for these outcomes. Data were collected immediately after birth and in a notary’s office where all deaths were registered. All newborns, including premature babies, were included. The aims of the study changed over time, following increasing exposure to life course literature and funding availability. In 1987–89, all schools (n = 76) in Ribeirão Preto were visited to find children born in 1978–79. Students enrolled in first to fourth grade were assessed to estimate the prevalence of infant malnutrition and obesity, to measure weight and height and to investigate the association of birthweight and social, pregnancy and neonatal variables with current nutritional status. In 1996–97, male military conscripts were assessed to study: the influence of early life factors on final height; the influence of early life factors (pregnancy, neonatal and school age) on nutritional status; the interaction of these early life factors with social factors in affecting nutritional status; and the conscripts’ schooling. The 2002–04 evaluation was characterized by broader objectives (the developmental origins of health and disease) but limited by reduced funding, which led us to choose a random sample of a third of the original cohort. It was also the first time that twin studies were included. The aims were to: determine whether intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is associated with the following risk factors for non-communicable chronic diseases in adults: obesity, sensitization to allergens, abnormalities of pulmonary function, arterial hypertension, abnormalities in coagulation factors and lipoproteins, hyperglycaemia, metabolic syndrome and asthma; determine the effect of some intervening factors, such as tobacco smoking, sedentary lifestyle, and alcohol and drug consumption, in the association between IUGR and a history of non-communicable diseases in adulthood; estimate the prevalence of metabolic syndrome in a young adult population; evaluate the effect of social mobility from birth to adulthood on adult non-communicable diseases; describe patterns of physical activity and of food consumption during young adulthood, according to socioeconomic and demographic characteristics; determine cohort mortality up to the age of 20 years and possibly related factors; investigate whether being born with IUGR and being overweight at school age increases body mass index during young adulthood; and assess any long-term effects of birth by caesarean section. Finally, the 2016–17 follow-up wave occurred after the establishment of a consortium with two other groups studying Brazilian birth cohorts, in Pelotas and São Luís. This wave involved new aims, such as: mental health and human capital; genetic, biological and behavioural risk factors of non-communicable diseases; and body mass composition, individual and family obesity and violence, bone mineral density, endothelial dysfunction, sleep pattern, oral health and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. Ribeirão Preto is located in the south-east of Brazil. Its population was 318 496 in 1978 and had grown to 694 000 in 2016. The city has a high human development index (0.79), a GDP per capita of US$13,680 and significant inequality (Gini Index 0.54). Its main activities are agribusiness, commerce and services. In 1978, it was called ‘the Brazilian California’, given the boom of biofuel production (alcohol) after the 1973 oil crisis. The 1978–89 cohort sample was drawn from all 9067 hospital births of liveborn infants (98% of all newborns) and included those whose mothers lived in Ribeirão Preto. After excluding newborns whose families were non-residents (about 20%), plus the 1% of mothers who refused to participate and 2.5% of mothers discharged from hospital before being interviewed, 6973 babies comprised the initial sample. The participants have been followed up for 37–39 years, with five assessments (Figure 1). The baseline comprised 6973 newborns. The first wave, or school age assessment, comprised 2861 participants. After discounting 257 infants who died in the first year of life, this figure corresponded to 43.5% of the original sample. The second wave, or assessment of male conscripts, comprised 2048 participants (61.3% of the initial cohort). The third wave, young adult assessment (23–25-year-olds), received financing for following up a third of the original cohort. It assessed 2103 participants (30.2%), of whom 40 were twins. The fourth wave, mature adult assessment (37–39-year-olds), involved 1775 participants, including 10 twins (32% of the available individuals). By that time, 458 of the initial cohort had died. Furthermore, participants with low birthweight or short length at birth, those who were born vaginally, and those whose mothers had low levels of education, were smokers or very young, or whose heads of family were in manual occupations, were less likely to be followed up. Analysis must take this into account. More than 90 MEDLINE-indexed papers have been published to date.1–91 Ribeirão Preto has had, over the period of our study, an infant mortality rate of 36.4%.18 Preterm birth and IUGR rates were 7.6%12 and 10.6%,22 respectively. Smoking during pregnancy was reported by 28.8% of mothers,84 and 30.3% experienced a caesarean delivery (CD).9 At school age, 6.4% of the children were obese; they were more likely to be singletons and to come from wealthier families.35 At 18 years, IUGR and weight gain during late childhood were identified as risk factors for obesity.25 In adulthood, excess weight was highly prevalent in men (30%) and associated with the metabolic syndrome.90 We also identified a large group of normal-weight individuals with this syndrome.57 Adult women who had suffered severe IUGR had higher carbohydrate intake.39 Some key findings relate to CD: the association of CD with increased rates of low birthweight and preterm birth (see commentary in IJE21), the increased number of CD due to the ‘physician factor’; and the association of CD with future adiposity and adult hypertension. Other findings were related to later consequences of early life events, such as the association of polycystic ovarian syndrome with being small for gestational age; the association of social mobility with adult obesity, and how it differed according to sex; the dejà vu of adolescent childbearing across generations; the association of asthma, depending on its definition, with obesity; and the description of a new adiponectin gene mutation associated with early onset of obesity and metabolic syndrome. The 1978 Ribeirão Preto cohort is the oldest population-based birth cohort in Brazil, and its members are now entering their fifth decade. Many data (sociodemographic, clinical, behavioural) and biological samples have been stored. Since the 1990s, the protocol has been identical to that of another Brazilian birth cohort of similar size (in Sao Luis, north-eastern Brazil, which is quite different in geography, culture and wealth). Both cities have been using the same methods and tools. In 1994 and 2010, both cities started two other birth cohorts, allowing for pooling and comparisons of many types of data. Since 2016, the Pelotas Birth Cohorts from southern Brazil have joined, and the cohort studies of the three cities have become a consortium. The first results have been published.82,84,85 During the first period of the cohort, results were published almost exclusively in national peer-reviewed journals. This is not a weakness, per se, but it delayed the establishment of international contributions and partnerships. An important weakness is the loss to follow-up—especially among mothers with lower levels of education and those of lower socioeconomic status—and the consequent attrition of participants being followed up. Contribution of Dry Forests and Forest Products to Climate Change Adaptation in Tigray Region, Ethiopia
records.abstract: Despite their ecological importance, dry forests’ contribution to climate change adaptation is often neglected. Hence, this study was initiated to assess the socioeconomic contribution of dry forests to climate change adaptation in Tigray Region, Ethiopia. A mixed quantitative and qualitative research design was used to examine the role of dry forests in climate change adaptation. Household questionnaire survey, key informants, and a focus group discussion were used to collect data. The results indicated that 94% of all households visited a dry forest at least once a month to access the forest and forest products. While the dry forest income level varied significantly (p < 0.05), the overall dry forest income level contributed to 16.8% of the total household income. Dry forest income enabled the reduction of the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve by 21% in dry evergreen Afromontane Forest users, by 3.02% in Combretum–Terminalia woodland users, and by 3% in Acacia–Commiphora woodland users. Gender, occupation, wealth status, and distance from the forest to their homes are all factors that significantly affected Combretum–Terminalia woodland users’ income level. Among Acacia–Commiphora woodland users, the respondents’ age influenced the dry forest income level, whereas, among dry evergreen Afromontane Forest users, the family size of the household influenced the dry forest income level. The findings of this study could help policy makers understand the crucial role of dry forest income in the livelihood of the community and in climate change adaptation. Policymakers could reduce the pressure on dry forests by introducing policies that recognize the role of dry forest income in reducing poverty and income inequality and by establishing farmer cooperation in commercializing the non-timber forest products which support the long-term coping and adaptation strategy. Further research is needed to understand the increasing role of dry forest products in climate change adaptation over time and its contribution to the national economy at large.

records.title: Physical Cues of Partner Quality
records.abstract: Abstract The dominant evolutionary theory of sexual attraction posits that attraction serves as a psychobehavioral and motivational mechanism for identifying healthy, fertile, and appropriate mates. According to this theory, humans and animals display cues that reflect their mate quality and, if successful, are perceived as attractive by potential mates. There is evidence for such valid cues in human faces, bodies, and non-bodily traits, which include adornments and items that signal provisioning ability, creativity, artistic skills, or conspicuous consumption. In this chapter, we discuss the evidence for the existence of these facial, bodily, and non-bodily cues and for their role in communicating aspects of partner quality, including health, fertility, developmental stability, genetic quality, and potential for parental investment. We further discuss sex differences in the physical cues that men and women rely on in mate choice. We conclude by highlighting the centrality and evolutionary importance of physical cues in contemporary sexual selection, and how they manifest in evolutionarily novel inventions such as physical self-enhancements, “sexy selfies,” social media, and online dating.

records.title: Prevalence and determinants of adolescent childbearing: comparative analysis of 2017–18 and 2014 Bangladesh Demographic Health Survey
records.abstract: Objectives: Bangladesh has one of the highest adolescent childbearing rates in South Asia, which prevent women from realizing their full potential in life. This study aimed to compare the prevalence and determinants of adolescent childbearing in Bangladesh using data from the 2014 and 2017-18 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS). Methods: Nationally representative surveys of respondents were selected using a two-stage sampling process. The study recruited 2,023 and 1,951 ever-married women aged 15-19 from 2014 and 2017-18 BDHS surveys, respectively, from rural and urban settings from all eight geographic divisions of Bangladesh. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression models were fit to determine the factors associated with adolescent childbearing. Result: The adolescent childbearing prevalence rate was 30.8% in 2014 BDHS and 27.6% in 2017-18 BDHS. Marriage at age 13 years or less also reduced significantly in 2017-18 compared to 2014 (12.7% vs. 17.4%, respectively). Significantly higher odds of adolescent childbearing were found in 2014 among women in the Sylhet Division (adjusted odds ratio (AOR) = 3.0; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.6-6.1) and the Chittagong Division (AOR = 1.8; 95% CI: 1.8-2.7) compared to the Barisal Region; however, in 2017, there were no significant differences was found across the geographic Divisions. Compared to women in the lowest wealth quintile, women in all other quintiles had lower odds of adolescent childbearing, with the lowest odds found among women in the wealthiest quintile (AOR = 0.3; 95% CI: 0.2-0.6). Women who married at age 14-17 had 60% lower odds of adolescent childbearing compared to the women who married at age 10-13. Conclusion: Nearly one-third of married adolescents in Bangladesh were pregnant or had at least one child in 2014, and it was reduced only marginally in 2017-18. Marriage at an early age and income inequalities among families were significant predictors of adolescent childbearing in Bangladesh. This study highlighted change in the magnitude and determinants of adolescent childbearing in Bangladesh taken data from two nationally representative surveys conducted 4 years apart.
